plain_english: Nick's Edge Dashboard. Research screen, not a trade signal. It sums six simple checks into one score per market.
Technicals + COT + Crowd + Growth + Inflation + Jobs. 7 or more Very Bullish, 4 to 6 Bullish, -3 to 3 Neutral, -4 to -7 Bearish, -8 or less Very Bearish.

54 markets, like EdgeFinder: 29 currency pairs (the 28 majors and crosses plus USDZAR), 8 currency indexes, 8 stock indexes (with the Russell 2000), the US 10-year Treasury note (US10T), gold, silver, platinum, copper, oil, natural gas, bitcoin and ether. The added markets are scored with the same rules as the market most like them: US10T and the Russell like the other US stock indexes, platinum and copper like silver, natural gas like oil, ether like bitcoin, and USDZAR like any other pair. The added markets can be switched off in Settings.

Top Setups splits that score into 18 factors, each a whole number from -2 to +2. 1 Day Change is today's score minus the score on the trading day before. On a Saturday or Sunday it shows Friday against Thursday, the same way EdgeFinder does. The factor coverage table says which countries have a free series. A zero there means no free series, or a print with no consensus.

A score snapshot is saved for every market every day. Days before the live job started were rebuilt from saved prices, COT reports and calendar releases. Retail crowd readings have no free history, so the crowd is only counted from the day the live readings started. Older days use the put/call ratio for US indexes and commodities, and 0 for the rest.

topic: Why a score can differ from EdgeFinder
plain_english: We use free data: Yahoo Finance prices, CFTC COT, IG client sentiment and Myfxbook crowd readings and the Nasdaq economic calendar. EdgeFinder uses its own paid feeds. Three things cause most gaps. 1) Some releases have no forecast on the free calendar, so they score 0 here (for example Canada's manufacturing PMI and Switzerland's services PMI). 2) EdgeFinder's prices close at a different hour, so a trend that is just turning can read +1 there and +2 here. 3) Where both sides have a forecast, EdgeFinder's forecast can differ from the free one, so a single cell can flip. EURUSD shows the rules match: on Oct 24 all 14 macro cells, COT, crowd and seasonality matched EdgeFinder, and only Trend differed. CADCHF (EdgeFinder +8) differs mostly because of points 1 and 3: Canada's PMIs have no free forecast, and Canada's retail sales and jobs, and Swiss GDP and PPI, scored differently on the free calendar.
Trend score (3-day average vs 14-day average, -2 to +2) plus seasonality (+1 if this month is usually up over 10 years, -1 if usually down).
Big speculators in futures (CFTC, weekly). For a pair: did the long share rise or fall for each side. For other markets: are they net long, and did the long share rise.

What retail traders hold. Most of them lose, so the score leans the other way. 60% or more long scores -1, 40% or less long scores +1, in between scores 0. A currency index uses that currency against the US dollar. A grey 0 marked no retail data means no free source had a reading for that market.

topic: Where the crowd numbers come from
plain_english: We check free public pages every hour, with no login. First IG client sentiment: the share of IG client accounts that are long each market (the same numbers DailyFX used to show). If IG has no number for a market, we use the Myfxbook community outlook, which Myfxbook offers free for other websites to show. A Myfxbook login is tried last, only if one is saved. If no source answers this hour, a reading up to 6 hours old is kept and marked saved. After that the market shows no retail data. If no retail source covers an index or commodity, the CBOE put/call ratio is used when that switch is on. Each source can be turned on or off in config.json, under retail_sources. The source and time are shown on the Retail sentiment page, on each scorecard, and under Top setups.
Latest release beat the forecast = +1, missed = -1, for each country. For a pair the second currency is subtracted.

Scored like EdgeFinder: we compare each central bank's policy rate today with the forecast for the end of this quarter. Forecast higher = +1, lower = -1, the same = 0. For a pair the second currency is subtracted, so GBPJPY is +1 when the Bank of England is expected to hike and the Bank of Japan is expected to hold. The forecasts come from the free Trading Economics forecast page and are checked every hour. If the page does not load, the last saved copy is used for up to 14 days. You can switch this off in config.json (interest_rate_forecast). Then the score goes back to the rate decision against its consensus, which is almost always 0 because banks rarely surprise.

US stock indexes, the 10-year note, gold, silver, platinum, copper, oil, gas, bitcoin, ether and the USD Index use the US 2-year Treasury yield for their Interest rate cell, like EdgeFinder. We compare the latest yield with its average over the last 7 trading days. If the yield is above its average it is rising. A rising yield is bad for stocks, bonds, metals, oil and crypto, so they get -1, and good for the US dollar, so the USD Index gets +1. A falling yield gives the opposite. The same number gives the same answer. The yield comes from FRED (DGS2). The US Treasury's daily yield file is the backup, and it also adds the latest day when FRED is a day behind. You can switch this rule off in config.json (two_year_yield_7day). Then the old rule is used: the 21-day average today against 5 days ago, and the USD Index goes back to the Fed forecast.

Carry is what you earn for holding a pair: the first currency's interest rate minus the second one's. The rate for every currency is its central bank policy rate, from the same free Trading Economics page the Interest rate score uses. The real yield is that rate minus the latest yearly inflation (CPI). If the page has no number for a currency, the FRED rate is used instead and the Carry page says so. You can switch this off in config.json (carry_policy_rates).

topic: Where the rate and yield numbers come from
plain_english: FRED (the St. Louis Fed) for the US 2-year and 10-year yields, the US real yield and breakeven inflation, and credit spreads. Each one has a free backup if FRED does not answer: the US Treasury for yields, the New York Fed for the US overnight rate, the ECB for the euro deposit rate, and the Bank of England for SONIA. Credit spreads have no free backup, so the last saved values are shown. The Updates log says which source was used each hour.

USDZAR can differ from EdgeFinder on interest rates. Both the Fed and the South African Reserve Bank have a higher forecast than today's rate on the free Trading Economics page (US 4.00% to 4.25%, South Africa 7.25% to 7.50% by the end of this quarter), so here they cancel out to 0. EdgeFinder showed +1 on Oct 24, so its South Africa forecast was likely flat. This is a difference in the data source, not in the rule.
A high-impact event for either currency in the next 24 hours. Times are Pacific Time (PT).
COT is out Fridays for the prior Tuesday. Prices are end of day plus the latest hourly snapshot.
